edition of Śrīdharadāsa’s *Sadukti-karṇāmṛta*. The abbreviations for those anthologies are as follows: *su.* = *Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa*.
sad. = *Saduktikarṇāmṛta*, subh. = *Subhāṣitāvalī*, sū. = *Sūktimuktāvalī*

The back of Ambikā’s hand, held in the *khaṭakāmukha* gesture drawn by the bowstring, is suffused with a mass of shimmering light from her fingernails.
May your sidelong glance protect you—a glance bearing the playful grace of a bee wandering about in longing for the ear-ornament of blossoming sprouts. (1) (Su.
Cast off when he clung to their hands, violently struck even as he seized the hem of their garments,
driven away as he grasped their hair, and ignored with agitation when he fell at their feet—
he who was repulsed even while embracing by the young women of Tripura, whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears.
May that arrow-fire of Śambhu, like a lover who has committed a fresh offense, burn away your misfortune.
(2) Bearing his disheveled mass of shimmering, dark curls and his swaying earrings... (Harabāṇa; Su. 49, Sad. 76)

May that face of the slender maiden protect you for a long time—her face with its slightly smeared tilaka, her eyes weary at the end of lovemaking, and moistened by very fine droplets of perspiration during the reversal of sexual positions; what need is there for deities such as Hari, Hara, and Brahmā? (3)

(Viparītarata— Sādhanamālā 1141, Śāradātilaka 3702) With glances languidly turned, moist with the moisture of love, repeatedly half-closed, for a moment directed toward him, flickering with shame, and averted by the closing of the eyes;
"Tell me, O charming girl, who is this fortunate man that you gaze upon today with eyes that seem to vomit forth the longing of the heart hidden within?
(4) (Vāsakasajjā; Su. 508; Sad. 658)

The favor toward her was granted by you alone, and she has been cherished by you for a long time; yet today, by fate, you yourself have indeed committed this new offense against her. This unbearable anger of hers clearly cannot be appeased by words of consolation.
Therefore, O friend, let her weep piteously with a voice released from all restraint.
Outside, the beloved of my life sits drawing figures on the ground with his head bowed;
my sisters remain without food, their eyes swollen from constant weeping.

All your laughter and recitations have been abandoned by the parrot-caged birds; such is your current state—O hard-hearted one, now relinquish your pride! (6) (The Awakening of the Friend; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 713)
"O slender one, women forcibly seize their lover and do not stay even when forbidden;
why then do you grieve and why do you weep in vain? Do not do what is pleasing to them."
O timid one, why are you being sold after being seized by hundreds of suitors— mere pebbles— who are themselves desirous of play, young, and sensitive, yet possess such a husband as that?
(7) (From the edition by Motilal Banarsidass, 1983)
Women, charming yet deceitful, captivate their lover and do not stay even when forbidden;
having bound him firmly with the noose of their soft, trembling vine-like arms in anger,
they lead him to the pleasure-chamber in the evening before their friends.
"Again, it was like this," he said, his voice faltering in soft tones as he confessed his misdeed;
the fortunate lover, intent on concealment, is indeed struck down by his weeping beloved—smiling all the while. (8) (The Deceitful Hero)
O beloved of the sun, will you come here at the end of the watch, or at midday, or even later than that, or perhaps when the entire day has passed?

Thus, with childish talk accompanied by tears falling from her cheeks, she prevents the departure of her beloved who wishes to go to a land reachable in a hundred days. (9) (The Frustration of Departure— Sūtra 532)
Sū 37.7) O beautiful one, do those who have departed not meet again? Why then do you worry for my sake?

When I said, "There is nothing to be done; I am utterly emaciated," she looked at me with eyes whose pupils were sluggish with shame and from which streams of tears fell, and by her smile, she revealed her resolve for the future death. (10)
Hearing at midnight the deep sound of a steady rain-cloud pouring forth water, a traveler,
long brooding with long-drawn sighs and tearful eyes upon his young wife separated from him,
wept aloud with an unrestrained throat throughout the entire night.
Just as the lodging of a traveler passing through a village is forbidden by the villagers;
O friend, when I somehow said "Go" out of playful anger— *Varṣāpathika*, Saduktikarṇāmṛta 915.

"He left his bed and departed by force, his heart as hard as stone"—when I think thus of that person who has violently destroyed our love and is devoid of compassion, my shameless mind runs back to him once more; what am I to do? (12) (15)
The words spoken by a married couple at night were overheard by their house-parrot; when he repeated them the next morning in the presence of his teacher,
the bride placed a fragment of ruby from her ear-ornament into the parrot's beak as an offering.
Afflicted by shame, she effects a verbal restraint under the pretext of a pomegranate fruit. (13) (16) (The Shame of the Parrot’s Speech, Kuvalayānanda 173)
Out of ignorance, you have embraced me while I was in distress, turning my face away from you due to humiliation. (Su. 621, Sad. 1180, Subh. 2214, Śā. 3743)
O fickle one, what have you gained here by bringing your good fortune to such a state?
Behold this chest of yours, reddened by the contact with your beloved’s breasts and their rubbed ointment, now marked by the impressions of her braid, variegated with the mud of dirt and oil. (14)
Sitting together on one seat was abandoned; even the sudden embrace was obstructed by the pretext of fetching betel-leaf from afar.
Not even a word was exchanged, as she occupied herself with the attendants nearby; thus, the clever woman rendered her anger fruitful by means of her subtle behavior toward her beloved.
(15) (Māninī, Saduktikarṇāmṛta 692; Rasārṇavasudhākara 2.67g)
Seeing his two beloveds seated upon a single seat, he approached them from behind with reverence; under the pretext of engaging in a playful dalliance,
he closed the eyes of one while his neck was slightly tilted and his hair stood on end, as his heart overflowed with love for her whose mind was radiant with affection.

The rogue kisses another woman, whose cheek-surface is radiant with a suppressed smile, while she remains averse to his advances because he has rejected her prostration at his feet. (Śaṭhanāyaka, Su. 603, Sad. 881)

Having been addressed with the words "O you who act like a silent rogue," and having been treated as a mere man by her lover as he departed in anger, she sighed deeply and, placing her hands upon her breasts,
cast a gaze veiled by tears toward her friends. (17)
(When the lover is proud, *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* 896:
Why is the lovely-eyed girl sleeping again with the edge of her garment held even more tightly by her girdle? Thus the beloved asks her attendants at will.

"Mother, she forbids me even to sleep here"— with these words, she who had harbored anger turned over on the bed under the pretext of sleeping and gave him an opening. (18) (The act of ascending the bed.)
77.11) On a single bed, they lay with their backs turned to one another, suffering in silence; though the conciliation was present in each other’s hearts, they both preserved their dignity.
As the eyes of the couple mingled through the gradual turning of their sidelong glances, the quarrel of pride was broken; they embraced each other's necks with laughter and impetuosity.
(19) (The shattering of pride; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 7.23)
"I see what she intends toward me"—thus did I maintain my composure;
"What is this rogue saying to me?"—thus did she resort to feigned anger. In that interval, they were both cleverly evasive with their mutual, embarrassed glances.

I laughed with feigned pretense, but she shed tears that robbed her of self-control; for when her pride had faded away, her moon-like face was held by her hand. (20) (Kuvalayānanda 185; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 1366) *uccāvacaṃ* (variegated). *parimlāne māne* (when her pride had withered). *mukhaśaśini* (upon her moon-like face). *karadhṛte* (held by her hand).
When I had exhausted all other means and was left with nothing but the single refuge of prostration,
she suddenly revealed her favor through tears that were blocked by the hollows of her eyelashes and then burst forth from the slope of her breasts. (21)
(Varied, Sad. 1367, Subh. 1608, Sū.
58.1) Why is her chest—marked with the seal of the embrace from the slopes of her breasts thickly smeared with unguents—concealed under the pretext of bowing at your feet?

When this was said, she cried out, "Where is that? and suddenly embraced me with impetuosity to wipe it away; under the power of that pleasure, even the slender girl forgot it. "O lovely-eyed one, you possess a captivating beauty even without your bodice. (22)
When her beloved said, "O Lakṣmī," and touched her anklet, the circle of female friends—
standing near the edge of the bed with smiling faces, their eyes filled with the joy of a festival—
departed slowly, making pretexts for their departure. (23) (27)
Even when a frown is fashioned, her gaze looks up with even greater longing; even when her heart is made stern, her body takes on a thrill of horripilation;
and even when her speech is restrained, this scorched face breaks into a smile.
When he has been seen, how can there be any fulfillment of pride toward that person?
(24) (Anuraktamāninī, Su. 695, Sad. 702, Subh. 1580; Uṇ. 5.25)

O beloved, pass even a few days with your eyes closed; may all be well with you until I close my own eyes while the quarters are not yet empty. We shall have returned by then, through the rising fortune of our circle of friends.
Tell me, what message do you have? What offering of a handful of water do you desire at these sacred fords? //25//
(Yātrākṣepa, Saduktikarṇāmṛta 7.31 [of the Heroine]) At the time of her husband's first offense, she— without the instruction of her friend— [acted].

She does not know how to express her agitation through the turning of her limbs or through indirect speech; with her lotus-eyes cast down and tears falling from the base of her clear cheeks, the young woman merely weeps, her tresses tossing as they drench her rolling eyes. (26)
(Act IV, Verse 498) "Enough! Let it be known. Cease these deceptive words, my dear; you may go.
There is not even the slightest fault in you; rather, fate is turned against us."

Since your love has reached such a state as this, what pain is there for us when this wretched life, naturally fickle, has departed? (27) (The words of an indignant woman; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 708; Padacandrikā 223)
A radiant necklace is placed upon your breast, a tinkling girdle is fastened around your firm hips, and jeweled anklets jingle at your feet; thus,
O charming girl, you go to meet your beloved like one who has struck a drum.
If you gaze at the quarters of the sky with a trembling born from some excessive fear: [I am he] who, having arrived every morning, caused sleeplessness in your eyes;
and who, now that I have become dull-witted, has produced a sense of lightness in you through the departure of my former dignity.
"What, you simpleton! Have I not done what was to be done? You have abandoned the thought of pleasure; go away!
You stand there in distress, yet you shall hear what I will now do for your own good.
"She is a young girl, while we are timid of heart; she is a woman, while we are full of fear."
She bears a pair of full and elevated breasts, yet we are burdened with weariness;
she is unable to walk due to her heavy hips, yet we have become incapacitated by faults belonging to other people—how strange! (30)
(The Favorable Hero;
The bracelets have set out; my dear friends have gone away forever;
not for a moment has she remained steadfast; her heart has resolved to go on ahead.
When the beloved has made up her mind to depart, everyone has set forth together.
When one must depart, why is this caravan of dear life and friends abandoned? (31) (The words of a woman whose husband is away;
Subhāṣitaratnakośa 1151)

37.19) Biting her sprout-like lower lip, trembling with fear, shaking the tips of her hands, and knitting her creeper-like eyebrows as she uttered words of anger: "Do not let me go, you rogue!"—she [spoke].

Those who have impetuously kissed the proud woman, whose eyes were tremulous with the sound of "śīt," have obtained nectar; the ocean was needlessly churned by the foolish gods. (32) (Kissing, Saduktikarṇāmṛta 1105, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1303, Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3668)
"Friend, he is asleep; let him sleep," saying this, my friends departed immediately thereafter.
Then, by me, who was softened by love and became simple-hearted, my face was placed upon his face.
When the rogue’s eyes were discovered to be falsely closed, I stood with my hair standing on end.
I was overcome with shame, and so she too was won over by me through methods appropriate for that moment.
In this [love], anger is the knitting of the brows; restraint is silence; conciliation is mutual smiling; and favor is a look of grace.

Behold now this very inconsistency of that love of mine: you roll at my feet, yet for me—a wicked woman—there is no release from my anger. (34) (The Indignant Woman [māninī] toward the Hero; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 709)
"O slender-limbed one, abandon your anger; look at me prostrate at your feet.
Indeed, never before has your anger been of such a kind.
When her lord spoke thus, she cast a sidelong glance with half-closed eyes.
Not a single drop of the abundant tears from her eyes was released.
(35) (The shattering of pride; Sadukti-karṇāmṛta 7.25) Her breasts were flattened by a deep embrace, causing a thrill of horripilation to break forth.

With the beautiful garment on her hips slipping down due to the excess of the essence of thick affection, crying out in thin, gasping syllables, "No, no, O giver of honor! Enough, enough!"—is she asleep, or is she dead, or has she merged into my mind, or has she dissolved away? (36)
When her husband touches the hem of her garment, she lowers her face with newfound modesty;
she desires a forceful embrace yet withdraws her limbs discreetly;
casting her eyes toward a smiling friend, she is unable to speak.
At the first jest, the newlywed bride faints within herself out of modesty. (37) (Navoḍhā; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 512, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 2056)

When the bond of affection has passed away, when the high esteem of love has dissolved, and when true friendship has ceased—just as one behaves toward a mere stranger—the person walks on ahead. (Śā. 3673; Viṣṇudās Uṇ. 5.19)
Therefore, O dear friend, as I reflect again and again upon those days that have passed, I know not what reason there is for my heart not to shatter into a hundred pieces.
(38) (uccāvacaṃ, su. 697)
For those two who have long been separated, whose limbs are now relaxed by the pain of longing,
and who after a long time again rejoice as if the world had been newly born, (the moon rises).
When the long day has somehow passed and the two have ascended to the night, the conversation between the young couple spreads so extensively that their passion does not equal it.
(39) A long garland of salutation has been fashioned by joy itself, not by blue lotuses.
No heap of flowers was fashioned with her smile, nor were jasmine and other blossoms offered;

no water from jars was given as an arghya-offering for the pair of her sweat-dripping breasts; rather, as she entered [the presence] of her beloved, the slender woman performed the auspicious rite with her own very limbs. (40)
When my lover, having committed an offense, lay down, I assumed the guise of my dear friend and approached; embracing him in error, I spoke of my secret longing for union with him.
To which he replied with a laugh, "O simple one, this is exceedingly difficult," and forcibly—
Having been embraced by that rogue at the onset of evening today, I have been led astray.
Suspecting my prostration, he respectfully covers his feet with the hem of his garment;
under some pretext he conceals his arrival, and he does not look directly at my smile.
When I speak to her, she converses with her friend using contrary words;
let alone her intense affection, even her pride has a charming way of arising.
As many words as she was taught by her friends with false speech—

Having quickly confessed their offenses before their husband, they immediately began to behave exactly as commanded by the Mind-born God; such is the indescribable, charming way of love, which is naturally adorned by innocence. (43)
Eager from afar, turning away upon his approach, expanding its gaze when he speaks,
reddening as he embraces, slightly knitting the creeper-like brows when her garment is seized,
and with eyes filled with tears of water at the moment of bowing at the feet— the glance of the indignant woman.

"Alas! The eye has become skilled in the art of fabrication toward its beloved, who has now committed an offense. When the lord of her life asked, "O charming one, why this extreme emaciation of your limbs? Why this trembling? And from where does this pale face with its wan cheeks come?"— [The verse continues: She replied: "O Lord of my life, it is not that I am angry; rather, I am truly distressed by the pain of your departure. For when you were departing, you did not even look back at me once, though I was standing right here before you. (45) She spoke thus, her voice faltering as she wept, her eyes filled with tears, and her heart overwhelmed by the sorrow of separation. Then, in order to dispel her grief, he spoke these words to her, his own heart likewise tormented by the fire of love. (46) "O beautiful one, do not grieve for me, who am so wretched. For what man, being wise, would ever abandon a woman such as you? (47) It is only because of the power of destiny that I have been separated from you. O fair-faced one, I swear by my life: I shall soon return to you, having fulfilled my purpose. (48) Having spoken thus, he departed, leaving her behind. She remained there, her body wasted by the fever of love, her mind fixed on him alone, and her very existence sustained only by the hope of his return. (49) Meanwhile, the king, having heard of her condition, sent messengers to fetch her. But she refused to go, saying: "I will not go until I have seen him. (50) Then, out of compassion, the king himself went to her. Seeing her in such a state, he spoke to her: "O daughter, tell me the truth. Who is this man for whose sake you have reached such a state? (51) She replied: "O King, he is no ordinary mortal. He is the son of the sage Kaśyapa, born of a doe, and is known as Rāma, the descendant of Raghu. It is for his sake that I have become so. (52) Hearing this, the king was filled with wonder and said: "If this is so, then let him be brought here. I wish to see him. (53) Thus, at the king's command, she was brought before him. Seeing her, the king was struck with amazement and spoke these words: "O daughter, tell me the truth. Is this indeed the son of Kaśyapa? (54) She replied: "Yes, O King, this is he. Then the king, having seen him, was filled with joy and honored him with great respect. (55) He then addressed Rāma: "O son, I have heard of your arrival. I have come here to see you. Please grant me an audience. (56) Rāma, having heard the king's request, agreed to see him. The king, accompanied by his ministers and retinue, entered the hermitage. (57) There he saw Rāma seated upon a seat of kuśa grass, his body emaciated by asceticism, yet radiant with spiritual splendor. (58) The king, having approached him with humility, bowed down and spoke: "O son of Kaśyapa, I am the king of Ayodhyā. I have come here seeking an audience with you. (59) Rāma, having greeted him with courtesy, invited him to sit. The king, having taken a seat, began to speak: "O sage, I have heard of your great power and your devotion to dharma. I have come here to seek your counsel. (60) Rāma replied: "O King, I am but a humble forest-dweller. What service can I possibly render to you? Yet, if it pleases you, I shall do whatever I can. (61) The king said: "O son of Kaśyapa, I have a great desire to see the ocean. Please grant me permission to travel there. (62) Rāma consented and said: "Very well, O King. I shall accompany you. Then, taking leave of the sage, they both set out together. (63) They traveled for many days until they reached the shore of the ocean. There, seeing the vast expanse of the sea, the king was filled with awe. (64) Rāma then spoke to him: "O King, behold the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa. It is here that

Having uttered, "All this arises from one's own nature," the slender girl, sighing as she turned away, released a flood of tears that spread between her eyelashes; meanwhile, I stood before the slender girl with my face bowed, startled by my slip of the tongue regarding her name. (45) [50]
Driven by embarrassment, that wretched man set about to draw something;
however, the arrangement of lines somehow transformed into such a form that the very same young woman appeared clearly once more through those distinct features.

The second half of this verse is as follows: Then, having recognized [him], the proud lady, with the luster of her throbbing, rosy cheeks and with a voice faltering from the sudden surge of deep affection, spoke.
"Aha! How wonderful, how wonderful, it is clear!"—having spoken thus, with eyes clouded by tears and filled with rage, he placed his left foot upon my head, discharging the Brahma-weapon.
O hard-hearted one, abandon this delusion based on false rumors; it is not right to bring suffering upon this person with the words of a slanderer. (Gotraskhalita, Sad. 686)
"What is this? Or rather, O innocent one, you have indeed made a firm resolve;
therefore, my dear, do as you please and remain at ease.
(47) Gently, the dust was laid to rest by the gale-force winds accompanied by the whirring of falling [leaves].

At the onset of the rainy season, drops of water fall, bursting forth like the unfolding leaves of the *kandala* plant; finding entry through the crevices of huts shattered by the force of the wind, they dispel the sweat upon the breasts of housewives preoccupied with their chores.

'The moon, appearing as a reflection within the cup, was drunk along with the honey after it had entered inside.'"
Surely he also pierced the darkness of pride within the hearts of the proud women, since she immediately became serene. (49)
This verse is also seen in the commentary on the Rudramadevakumāra [work] (Madhupāna, Sadukti-karṇāmṛta 10.89; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 2022; Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3648).
Seeing the beauty of clouds gathered in the sky, she somehow managed to say half a word, "O beloved, if by good fortune you are departing," while clutching my garment and scratching the earth.
She imitated that [state] wherein words have ceased.
This verse is also seen in the commentary of Vemabhūpāla:
"She, with tremulous and long eyes, and with heavy, lofty, and full breasts..."
My beloved, whose gait is languid from the weight of her broad hips, is the one who takes away my life.
The noble Arjunavarman considers this verse to be an interpolation:
"With her foot, adorned with a tinkling anklet, tender as a fresh sprout and dyed with red lac, languid with passion— "
He who is struck by his beloved out of affection is accepted as a true follower by the Lord Makaradhvaja.
This verse is found exclusively in Vemabhūpāla’s commentary:
(Anukūlanāyaka, Saduktikarṇāmṛta 873, Sūtra 85.1) "O young girl, O mistress, release your anger; what have I done to you out of wrath?"

"Have you no pity for us? It is not you who has offended me; all offenses lie with me. Why then do you weep with faltering words? Before whom are you weeping? Is it not before me? You say, 'I am not your beloved,' and for that reason you weep. (53)

Carrying away and scattering in great abundance toward the quarters of the sky the pollen of *kunda* flowers—pollen that has become saturated with a drizzle of cold dewdrops, which delights the bees and is exceedingly fragrant—those who are full of pride [the winds]. (Māninī, Saduktikarṇāmṛta 691; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1614)
These wintry winds blow, rising from the impact of the jar-like breasts smeared with saffron, as they drink in through the hissing mouths of the girls with eyes like young fawns.
This verse is also seen in the commentary on the *Rudramadevakumāra*:

"Having heard at midnight the thundering of fresh clouds, the slender woman fell from her bed onto the surface of the ground with loosened limbs; she was held by the hand by her distressed female companions."
Longingly, with her throat unbound, as the drops of her tears are shattered by the impact against the surface of her firm breasts,
the wife of the traveler weeps again and again, remembering the soft, faltering words of her beloved.
This verse is seen only in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) by Rudramadevakumāra:
"Why was my lord not embraced around the neck by me, a fool?
Why was this movement of the face not used for a kiss while he was kissing? Why was he not looked upon?"
"Why was it not said?"—thus brooding over the behavior of her new bride, the young woman, once passion has arisen, feels remorse as she recognizes the true flavor of love.
(56) (uccāvacaḥ, sad. 1369, subh. 2143)

When that lord of my life has arrived and stands eagerly embracing my neck— he whose very name, when heard, causes my limbs to break out all over in thick, manifest horripilation, and upon seeing whose moon-like face this body of mine becomes like a moonstone— [then...]
"When will my pride, which is as hard as adamant, finally be shattered?

[When will it be broken] by the moon-like faces of lovely women, drenched with drops of perspiration, shaking and tossing their creeper-like, dangling tresses, and causing the garments on their hips to flutter? (57) (59)

In the springtime, at dawn, the breeze blows— charming with the fragrance of the mass of pollen from rows of lotuses blooming to their heart's content, and removing the exhaustion born of the pleasures of love.
This verse also occurs in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Rudramadevakumāra*: "The body is as soft as a sandalwood-white sprout, and the lower lip is copper-red from betel...
(Prābhātikavāta; Sadukti-karṇāmṛta 459).
The limbs are tender like sandalwood-white shoots, and the lower lip is reddish-brown from betel.

At the onset of the afternoon in summer, when the eyes are stained turbid by the sprinkling of water from a fountain and the collyrium has been washed away; when the hair is moist with fragrant flowers and the garment clings to every limb, the loveliness of the body’s downy hairs is brought to perfection.
This verse is also seen in the commentary on the Rudramadevakumāra:
"Better is this day and not the night; indeed, better is the night and not the day."
Or rather, let both of these come to an end—that which is separation from beloved people. // 60 //
This verse is found only in the commentary on the Rudramadevakumāra:
"With tremulous tears from their eyes, with oaths, and with prostrations at his feet, those other wretched women try to turn back their beloved lord of their lives as he departs."
"May it be an auspicious day, a blessing, a fortunate morning for you as you set out;
O dearest one, once you have departed, you shall hear that which was desired by us and is worthy of our affection. (61) (The Obstruction of the Departure)
(As recorded in *Sadukti-karṇāmṛta* 7.35, *Subhāṣitāvalī* 1060,
*Śārṅgadharapaddhati* 3395, and *Sūktimuktāvalī* 37.12: Her creeper-like arm was clung to the hem of her garment, but it was not placed upon the threshold of the door.
She did not say the words "fall at my feet" or "stay"; yet,
when the time came and the sky was darkened by clouds, that rogue set out to depart,
only to be held back by his beloved with a flood of tears fashioned into a river.
(The Refutation of Departure;
Satyasiddhiśāstra 922,
Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 1057, Śālistamba-sūtra 3388, Sūtrālaṃkāra 37.5)
I do not know whether, when my beloved has arrived before me and speaks endearing words, all my limbs become ears—or rather, eyes. (63) (The heroine’s longing; Saduktikarṇāmṛta 960)
Love, made harsh by separation, makes your body emaciated;
and Yama, the merciless one, is counting the days. You too, O Lord, have fallen under the sway of the disease of pride—consider this, indeed!

O beloved, you who have been clinging to my feet for so long here, what kind of perversity is this?

"What offense has been committed against a beloved person who stands upon the path of righteousness and yet is angry?"—as she spoke these words of reproach, the force of her anger subsided; thereafter, with the breaking forth of tears, she neither remained still nor did she depart. (65)
In the past, this body of ours was certainly one and indivisible; from that, you became our beloved and we too were your most beloved, though our hopes were dashed.
Now you are our lord and we are your wife—what more can be said?
"By me has been attained this fruit of lives as hard as a thunderbolt. O simple one, why do you begin to spend all your time in such simplicity?
Assume pride, maintain your resolve, cast away your straightforwardness toward your beloved."
Thus enlightened by her friend, she, with a frightened face, spoke this reply to her:
"Speak softly; surely that lord of my life resides within my heart and will hear.
For since the moment he was drunk by me, who was parched with the thirst of love..."
From that time on, my thirst for the abundant nectar of that beloved’s lower lip has doubled; there is a certain wondrous thing in that, for it remains insatiable.

"O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, where are you going in the dense darkness of night, there where dwells that person dearer than life to me?"

Struck by a lotus in play, his lip bitten fearlessly by another woman, he stood with eyes closed as if his sight were offended by the filaments; she,

"Because the mass of sandalwood powder has been crushed by our tight embrace,
this bed is now rough," saying this, O lady of delicate limbs, you placed me upon your chest; then, with a distressed agitation, you pressed my toes between your firmly grasped lips.

When her beloved had somehow managed to refuse her with a faltering reply, she, emaciated by separation, feigned that he had not heard her by making an excuse. What was appropriate for a rogue—he did not pull back his own garment—but rather proceeded to do exactly that. (72) (74)
With her gaze fixed upon the empty house, she sighed again with agitation at the thought that her friend’s ears had overheard her indiscretion;

When the paths were obscured at the close of day and the darkness was spreading, the traveler’s wife, overcome with grief, took one step toward her home; at that very moment, she looked back again with her neck turned sharply, thinking, "May he not have arrived. (74)
When her beloved arrived after many hundreds of longed-for dreams, she spent the day somehow with her attendants—
fools whose cleverness had vanished— engaging in long conversations; then,

With a mind anxious for love, the slender-limbed woman extinguished the lamp by grasping a cluster of blossoms on a mango tree at the edge of the courtyard garden— a cluster beautified by female bees humming and clinging to the thick, spreading pollen. (75) (77)
I think that young girl, having covered her body with a fragment of her upper garment, weeps as the rising of her sighs causes her breasts to tremble, obstructing the sound of her throbbing throat.
She has heard with confidence the words of one who was prepared to depart: "I shall go. (76) (78)

Though he has gone far away and been neglected, even as he stands turning back again and again, I remain in this empty house; yet these vital breaths of mine are firm. O friends, stay! I am intent on living; I weep out of mere pretense. (77)
Having observed that the bedchamber was empty, she rose slightly from her bed and,
approaching the pretext of sleep, gazed for a long time at the face of her husband as he lay there quietly.
Having kissed her confidently, he beheld her cheek covered in horripilation; then, as the young woman lowered her face in shame, she was kissed for a long time by her laughing beloved.
(78) With her creeper-like brow quivering, she shook her head to indicate the direction of her rival.

No thrill has arisen, my breasts have not trembled, my body has not bristled with hair,

"Let us go; let there be going, or let it be otherwise. That very path of my mind which followed me for so long has become something else, O friend; for whom are men truly familiar? (100)

Falling at her feet, friendly conversation, charming flatteries, a firm embrace from the slender-bodied one, and forceful kissing— such indeed is the fickle onset of jealous anger; yet, even so, I do not dare to act.
"My beloved, dear to my heart, what indeed can I do in this matter?
(101) Having been summoned by him with the words "I have something to tell you," I sat down nearby in a secluded place and, because of my affectionate nature, became attentive.
Then, O friend, as he whispered something into my ear, I smelled his face, seized him by the braided hair, and firmly grasped his lower lip—
my mind being intent on the joy of his gaze while I contemplated the means for our acquaintance.
When passion has reached its peak and the messenger girl’s presence is fully blossoming before one’s eyes,
let alone the attainment of the joy of an impetuous embrace from the beloved— merely wandering through the street near her house brings about the highest bliss. (103)
When my beloved approached the bed, the knot of my garment loosened of its own accord from its binding,
and the cloth remained only slightly upon my hips, held by the strands of my loosened girdle;
O friend, this much I know now, but as for what happened during his embrace of my body, I know nothing more.
"Who is this? Where am I? What is my delight, or how did it come to be?"—not even the slightest memory of this remains to me.
For one afflicted by separation from her, she is in the palace; she is in every direction; she is behind me and she is before me; she is on the couch and she is on every path.
O mind! There is no other nature whatsoever belonging to me;
that, that, that, that, that, that—what is this doctrine of non-duality in the entire world? (105)

Wiping away your tears again and again with the tip of your fingernail, why do you weep in silence, O angry woman? You shall weep much more loudly when your pride has reached its ultimate limit through the words of that slanderer’s counsel.
Disgusted with his advances, my beloved will become indifferent. My face is turned down toward her face, my gaze is fixed upon her feet,
and my ears— most eager for her words— are closed to others.
Covered by my hands, the horripilation and the breaking of sweat upon my cheeks have appeared;
O friends, what shall I do, for the seams of my bodice are splitting into a hundred pieces?
That which was not removed by conciliation and was not restrained by the words of dear friends— [that very thing now torments me]. (11)
That pride which had been maintained with great effort for many long days through enduring hardship—
once their glances were somehow cast askance as they looked into each other’s faces, that pride was abandoned by both of them with a laugh, its former transgression utterly forgotten. (42)
At night, a traveler, distressed by the sound of clouds heavy with rain and shedding tears, sang out of longing a song that betrays the sorrow of his own separation;
let alone the mere mention of talk about wandering abroad, which robs one of life.
Just as the world has now hastily offered a libation of water to pride itself,
O fickle-hearted one, why was your beloved— come to your home of his own accord, fallen at your feet, and drenched with the moisture of love— so utterly neglected? (54)
Therefore, from now on for as long as you live, with the rise of happiness cast aside and with weeping as your only refuge, endure the fruit of the wrath of those ill-born ones.
Let alone placing trust in friends; even toward a person who knows the essence of your intentions, [trust is misplaced]. (56)
Even there, I am unable to cast my well-composed gaze upon her due to shame;
this world, moreover, is clever at mocking others and is fully capable of discerning subtle gestures.
O Mother, to whom shall I go for refuge? The fire of passion has grown old within my heart. (63)

"O beautiful one, why is this body of yours— immovable due to the delusion of the heavy burden of many thoughts, causing such trepidation even when merely being gazed upon, and adorned with ornaments that are themselves surpassed by its natural beauty?
(65) Thus questioned by her beloved, she, overwhelmed by pride, somehow suppressed her tears and stammering voice within herself.
When the bride simply said, "Nothing at all," how much was she not thereby describing to him?
O simple one, why did you suddenly display jealous anger toward your beloved, without considering the consequences of love and disregarding the advice of your friends?
For these very coals, whose flames blaze with the fire of separation, have been drawn toward you by your own hand; therefore, enough now with weeping in the wilderness.
